question: Did the founding emails form a binding contract that OpenAI would remain a nonprofit?
summary: The single most consequential factual question in the case.
plaintiff_position: Yes. The May–June 2015 emails (Exs. 1, 2), Brockman's November 2015 'bootstrap' email (Ex. 3), the certificate of incorporation, and the September 2017 reaffirmations together manifest a definite agreement that OpenAI would be a 501(c)(3), open-source, non-profit-inurement institution.
defense_position: No. There is 'no one single document that consists of a contract' (Dkt #163 p.2). At most the emails are aspirational; Musk's September 20, 2017 ultimatum (Ex. 13) and his pattern of donations are equally consistent with charitable solicitation, not contracting. Savitt opening: 'There isn't a single email or a single text message or any other document where Mr. Musk claims that OpenAI was obligated to remain a nonprofit.' (042826TT.txt:2698)
record: The court dismissed the express-contract count without leave but allowed the implied-in-fact contract to survive on the same emails. The PI ruling characterized the underlying charitable-trust question as 'a toss-up'. Whether the emails 'constitute a writing sufficient to constitute an actual contract or charitable trust… is debatable.' (Dkt #121 p.13)

question: When Altman wrote 'i remain enthusiastic about the non-profit structure!' on September 21, 2017, was that statement false when made?
summary: The former fulcrum of the fraud theories; still relevant as background to trust, reliance, and limitations.
plaintiff_position: Yes. By July 2017, Sutskever's biweekly update (Ex. 11) listed 'Designing the for-profit structure' as ongoing work; the September 20 'highest-stakes conversation' from Sutskever and Brockman discussed the for-profit structure in detail. The reaffirmation was a calculated representation made to keep Musk's money flowing while planning the conversion. ~$10.275M in continued contributions followed.
defense_position: Statements were truthful expressions of present belief and feeling. Musk himself was simultaneously demanding 'unequivocal initial control' of a for-profit; the team's resistance was to Musk's control demands, not to a continuing nonprofit ethos. The September 2017 emails were earnest attempts to preserve the institution Musk wanted.
record: The court found the statement 'actionable non-puffery' under Rule 9(b) and the fraud claim later survived MSJ. But on Apr 24, 2026, the court deemed fraud and constructive fraud voluntarily dismissed with prejudice. The statement remains evidentiary background, not a standalone live claim.

question: Why did Musk leave the OpenAI board in February 2018?
summary: Plaintiffs' 'sidelined' framing vs. defense's 'walked away' framing.
plaintiff_position: Musk stepped back as the for-profit architecture took hold; he was 'out of the picture' and 'OpenAI, Inc.'s Board stacked with compliant allies' (FAC ¶312).
defense_position: Musk demanded 'unequivocal initial control' of any for-profit OpenAI or absorption into Tesla. When Altman, Brockman, and Sutskever refused, Musk quit. Counterclaim ¶3: 'In 2017 and 2018, Altman, Brockman, and Sutskever refused to bow to Musk's demands for control of the enterprise or, alternatively, its absorption into Musk's electric car company, Tesla. So Musk quit.'
record: Musk's own deposition and trial testimony confirms he asked for 'unequivocal control' (042926TT.txt:3763). Sutskever's contemporaneous September 2017 email confirms the team's 'highest-stakes conversation' was about Musk's would-be unilateral control. The narrative gap is which party caused the break.

question: Did Musk himself propose making OpenAI a for-profit?
plaintiff_position: No, not in any binding sense. Trial testimony: 'I don't object to a for-profit that's in service to the nonprofit.' (042926TT.txt:6039)
defense_position: Yes. Musk privately advised it would be 'better to have a standard C corp with a parallel nonprofit' (¶24 of OpenAI's counterclaim). Earlier, his own December 2016 Neuralink-related email said: 'Setting it up as a nonprofit might, in hindsight, have been the wrong move.' (DX 559). Day 7 direct added Brockman's account that Musk said the nonprofit 'was the right one early on' but 'may not be the right one now,' that China's AI push was 'another reason to change course,' and that the Dota breakthrough was 'the triggering event' for the next structural step.
record: Documentary evidence supports the proposition that Musk advocated structural change at the time. The Day 7 trial record sharpened that point with testimony about July-August 2017 texts and emails tying Musk's shift to funding pressure, competition, and the Dota result. The contested issue remains whether those discussions undermined his reliance on the September 2017 reaffirmations or were conditional on him having control of the resulting entity.

question: Does Microsoft exercise de facto control over OpenAI?
summary: Central to plaintiffs' remaining aiding-and-abetting theory against Microsoft.
plaintiff_position: Yes. Microsoft holds the exclusive cloud relationship, exclusive licenses to GPT-4 and successors, $13.75B cumulative investment, and used its leverage to force Altman's reinstatement in November 2023. Nadella's quoted statement that Microsoft has 'all the IP rights and all the capability' ('We have the people, the compute, the data, everything') captures the position. Day 7 Wu testimony added that the 2023 JDCA licensed Microsoft all IP and technology except AGI, and that the Watershed MOU would give Microsoft certain product-IP access after a third-party AGI determination.

plaintiff_citations.snippet: licensed them all IP and technology... excluding only AGI

defense_position: No. Microsoft did not receive 'a conventional equity ownership interest' but a capped-return arrangement (Dkt #329 p.10). The 2019 partnership was 'arm's-length negotiations between sophisticated parties'; Microsoft 'remained supportive of its strategic partnership' and has not 'diverted the partnership benefits for its own benefit'.
record: Microsoft's MSJ and proposed findings characterize the relationship at length. Plaintiffs' November 2023 evidence remains partly under seal; the public record shows operational entanglement but not a judicial finding that it equals control. Wu's Day 7 deposition sharpened the economic and licensing picture but did not itself resolve the legal control question.

record_citations.snippet: total target redemption amounts... rounded to $250,000,000,000

question: Was there an OpenAI / Microsoft 'fund-no-competitors' covenant aimed at xAI?
summary: The basis of the dismissed antitrust counts.
plaintiff_position: Yes — investors were conditioned not to back xAI or other competitors. Plaintiffs cite a Financial Times article reporting investor calls.
defense_position: Restricting confidential information sharing to non-competing investors is industry standard and pro-competitive (Altman declaration). xAI raised over $11B — strong evidence the alleged boycott did not in fact restrain capital formation.
record: The court rejected the boycott theory at the PI stage: 'plaintiffs have provided no direct evidence of a horizontal agreement to boycott… xAI admitted that it could not provide a single declaration from an investor to confirm its theory.' (Dkt #121 p.8) Resolved against plaintiffs.

question: Was Musk's February 2025 $97.375B Letter of Intent a genuine acquisition offer or a 'sham bid'?
plaintiff_position: Genuine. Litigation-functional communication; if accepted, several claims would have been moot.

plaintiff_citations.title: MTD Counterclaim Order — LOI bears 'functional connection'

defense_position: Sham. The LOI was 'designed to disrupt Counterclaim Plaintiffs' relationships with current and prospective investors and has rendered the performance of those business relationships more costly and burdensome' (Counterclaim ¶119). The bid required OpenAI's board to 'expend significant resources in responding to it'.
record: On Day 5 of trial, Birchall testified the LOI 'was an investment… purely a business deal' and conceded 'Mr. Musk didn't give [me] that number'. The court struck Birchall's LOI testimony entirely; the bench colloquy: 'You must be very convincing. You're not convincing today.' (043026TT.txt:7775; motion to strike 050126TT.txt:294)

question: When did Musk's fraud / constructive-fraud claims accrue?
summary: Determines whether the August 2024 complaint is timely.
plaintiff_position: January 2023, when Microsoft's $10B investment closed and Musk testified he 'finally came to the conclusion… that OpenAI was really going to become… a profit-maximizing, closed-source organization'.
defense_position: By 2019 at the latest. Musk knew of the for-profit subsidiary in March 2019 (received the press release and term sheet); his September 2020 tweet ('OpenAI is essentially captured by Microsoft') is conclusive notice. Three-year limitations expired 2022; Musk did not sue until August 2024.

defense_citations.snippet: OpenAI is essentially captured by Microsoft.

record: On the Sept 22, 2020 cross: 'And you didn't come to court in 2020, did you?' — A: 'No, because he assured me that they were staying on mission, that they would continue to be a nonprofit and that OpenAI would be open source.' (043026TT.txt:2438)

question: Did Musk donate $1B (as he publicly pledged), $44.56M (the FAC tally), or $38M (the trial chart)?
summary: The 'tale of two Elons' — the gap between pledge and contribution is rhetorically central.
plaintiff_position: Trial chart: $38,191,066 in cash to OpenAI, plus office overhead, recruitment, and Tesla gifts in appreciation of the staff; the FAC alleges $44.56M total wired to OpenAI Inc.
defense_position: Of a publicly pledged $1B, Musk contributed less than 4 percent. Savitt: 'Mr. Musk fell $960 million short.' (042826TT.txt:2736)
record: Both numbers are correct. Public pledge was $1B; cash contribution was ~$38–$44.56M. The interpretive question is whether Musk's pledge created any expectation of full performance.

question: Did Altman and Brockman receive equity/financial benefits from the for-profit conversion?
summary: Plaintiffs allege private inurement; defense filings include redactions on equity figures.
plaintiff_position: Yes. The FAC alleges Altman and Brockman received equity in for-profit entities (¶ 374-375). Trial testimony emphasized that Brockman contributed 'zero' financial capital to the nonprofit, acquired his for-profit stake for $0, and now holds roughly $30B in OpenAI equity.

plaintiff_citations.snippet: you invested $0 in order to acquire that interest

defense_position: OpenAI MSJ pages on this are heavily redacted. Defense framing: any executive equity is at the for-profit subsidiary, structured around mission-aligned compensation; no improper inurement to the nonprofit.
record: Substantive equity figures and ownership percentages remain redacted in the public MSJ filings, but Brockman's trial testimony put at least his approximate current stake and $0 acquisition price in front of the jury.

question: Did Musk control OpenAI's office space (the Pioneer Building)?
summary: Defense exhibit highlighted at trial; relevant to private inurement and control narratives.
plaintiff_position: Musk paid the rent through his family office as part of his charitable support (FAC ¶425).
defense_position: Musk Industries controlled the Pioneer Building lease. Birchall to Sam Teller, Jan 2017 (DX 600): 'Elon holds 100 percent of the power and authority regarding the building.' Musk to Birchall, June 2016 (DX 539): 'I don't want Sam on the lease.' (043026TT.txt:5787, 5829)
record: The defense documentary exhibits go to the lease holder and decision rights. Whether this control supports plaintiffs' or defense's broader theory is contextual.

question: Has the 'capped-profit' structure been removed?
summary: Plaintiffs cite the 2024–2025 restructuring as completing the conversion.
plaintiff_position: Yes. 'The profit cap has been completely removed, and the clause that has the for-profit dissolving upon discovery of artificial general intelligence has also been removed, which is a very big deal.' (Musk testimony 042826TT.txt:5850) Day 7 Wu testimony said OpenAI's mission strategy committee began considering inverting the LLC waterfall into uncapped corporate stock as early as April or May 2024, and identified the non-binding Watershed MOU as the proposed recapitalization term sheet.

plaintiff_citations.snippet: Under the Watershed construct... certain access to certain product IP

defense_position: The restructuring 'is not a conversion of the nonprofit into a for-profit entity — as Musk has falsely and repeatedly claimed — but a structure change in which the nonprofit would continue to exist and pursue its mission… while the capped-profit would become a public benefit corporation' serving the same mission. (Counterclaim ¶77)
record: Substantive evaluation of the restructuring requires the closing documents, which appear in the redacted MSJ exhibit set. The court has not adjudicated the merits. The Day 7 record distinguishes the current 2023 JDCA license (all IP and technology except AGI) from the non-binding Watershed MOU, under which Microsoft would receive certain product-IP access after AGI is determined by a third-party panel.

question: Is the jury authorized to consider AI-extinction risk evidence?
summary: The court's scope rulings narrow the trial dramatically.
plaintiff_position: Plaintiffs sought to introduce extinction-risk testimony from Stuart Russell and others to contextualize OpenAI's mission and breach.
defense_position: Such testimony is irrelevant to the legal question and unduly prejudicial.
record: Excluded. The court: 'This is not a trial on the safety risks of artificial intelligence… The question here is whether there was a breach of charitable trust.' (043026TT.txt:817) 'Issues of extinction have been excluded.' (043026TT.txt:712) Ruling stands.

question: Was Musk ever a 'member' of OpenAI within the meaning of California Corp. Code §5710 (derivative-suit standing)?
summary: Doctrinal question that defeated the derivative claims.
plaintiff_position: Yes — at the time of the relevant conduct, before he resigned in February 2018.
defense_position: The statute requires current membership; Musk and Zilis were not members at the time of filing.
record: The court accepted the defense reading: 'That Musk and Zilis may have been members at one point is insufficient as a matter of law.' (Dkt #121 p.16) Counts XXII–XXIV dismissed without leave.

question: If plaintiffs win, who can receive restitution or disgorged gains?
summary: The late pretrial remedy fight created a standing/remedy tension.
plaintiff_position: Musk says he will not seek an award to himself, xAI, or a controlled fund. His preferred remedy is an award to the OpenAI charity directly, or to donor-advised funds that must donate the award to the OpenAI charity.
defense_position: Defendants say the waiver confirms the case lacks personal injury and that restitution normally restores value to the plaintiff, not a third-party charity. They ask the court to require a fuller waiver or treat the remedy defect as fatal.
record: PTO #3 assigns disgorgement to the Court as equitable relief. PTO #4 bifurcates liability and remedies. The court has not finally decided recipient or amount; May 1 trial commentary suggests reluctance to give an advisory redirect ruling before liability.

question: Do donor-advised funds and YC.org break Musk's standing or control over the donated property?
summary: OpenAI's cleanest technical defense to a Musk-specific trust corpus.
plaintiff_position: Musk treats himself as the funding source and settlor: the money was solicited from him, contributed because of OpenAI's stated charitable mission, and traceable into OpenAI's assets regardless of DAF routing.
defense_position: OpenAI says all cash contributions were indirect through DAFs and YC.org, that Musk relinquished ownership/control when he donated to those intermediaries, and that OpenAI recorded zero donor-restricted assets.
record: The public docket establishes the parties' positions but not the final factual resolution. This issue directly affects trust formation, restitution, and Musk's verified waiver.

question: Does Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §17510.8 create an independent charitable-trust path here?
summary: A late jury-instruction/legal issue over charitable solicitations.
plaintiff_position: Yes. Musk says Altman's 2016 funding requests and OpenAI CFO Chris Clark's July 2020 rent request were charitable solicitations; §17510.8 creates a fiduciary relationship and charitable trust upon acceptance.
defense_position: No. OpenAI says §17510.6 excludes solicitations within a charity's membership, Cohen v. Kabbalah Centre controls, and the July 2020 rent email was at most a $580,000 rent-specific request already used for rent.
record: The trial-wiki Day 5 summary says the court signaled §17510.6 controls over §17510.8, but the primary docket currently captures the dispute through the competing April 30 briefs rather than a written order.

question: Did Microsoft know about Musk-specific charitable-trust duties and substantially assist a breach?
plaintiff_position: Musk's proposed findings say Microsoft knew OpenAI's charitable obligations from diligence, the public charter/mission materials, and the 2023 board crisis, then assisted by funding and structuring transactions that enriched private investors.
defense_position: Microsoft's proposed findings say it was not involved in OpenAI's formation or Musk's departure, was not told of Musk-specific donation conditions, received contractual assurances, and did not cause any alleged breach.
record: The MSJ ruling left the claim alive, but Microsoft's April 27 proposed findings preserve no-knowledge, no-assistance, limitations, laches, and unclean-hands defenses. Wu's Day 7 testimony gives the jury concrete evidence on Microsoft economics and license scope, but it is still only part of the actual-knowledge / substantial-assistance inquiry.

question: Is Musk pursuing the case to restore a charity or to punish a competitor and its principals?
summary: A motive/bias dispute sharpened by the May 3 pretrial-communication application.
plaintiff_position: Musk says the case is about enforcing OpenAI's public charitable mission and preventing private enrichment from charitable assets.
defense_position: OpenAI says Musk is attacking a competitor. It seeks to introduce Brockman testimony that Musk told him before trial that Brockman and Altman would become the most hated men in America if they continued defending the case.
record: The application at #522 is a request to admit evidence, not a merits finding. It is still important because it shows how OpenAI intends to use motive and bias evidence during Brockman's testimony.
